HCM is characterized by myocyte disarray, with loss of the normal parallel alignment. This gives the myocardium a flattened appearance on endomyocardial biopsy.  Familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is caused by autosomal dominant mutations in the cardiac myosin-binding protein C or in the regulatory beta-subunit of cardiac troponin I or T. Recessive and dominant forms of autosomal gene mutations that lead to the substitution of alanine for threonine at position 68 (A68T) in the beta-myosin have been described. A68T mutations reduce the compliance of the cardiac sarcomere, leading to HCM.  Alternatively, a missense mutation in the troponin I or T subunit has been described whereby the cross-bridge cycling speed is increased, favouring the development of HCM. During translation, the mRNA is used to create proteins via the ribosomes. There are two types of RNA produced during transcription:mRNA and tRNA.mRNA is used in translation. Its function is to carry the amino acid chain which is made in the cytoplasm, out of the nucleus, through the nuclear membrane and into the cytoplasm of the cell. It is here where translation takes place and where the amino acids are assembled into proteins. Each mRNA molecule usually forms a single protein chain. But some mRNAs form more than one protein chain. These are called poly(ORFs).Some ORFs undergo splicing. Splicing is the removal of introns (non-coding material) from the mRNA. Introns are removed so that the remaining parts (exons) can be joined together to make a continuous mRNA. This is useful since most of the exons code for protein whilst many of the introns do not.
